title: Continuity Vault for Solo Operators
one_liner: A break-glass vault, dead-man switch and runbook so a solo business survives its owner's hospitalization or death, and its AI agents stop cleanly.
customer: Solo and two-person business owners aged 45+, reached through independent life-insurance agents, estate attorneys, SBA lenders and CPAs.
problem: For the majority of small businesses that are solo operations, the owner is the only person with access to the bank, domain, Google listing, payroll, customer list and payment processor. When the owner is incapacitated, nobody can legally or technically act. Delegated AI agents and OAuth tokens add new failure modes because they keep acting, or fail, without supervision.
solution: An encrypted vault with a named successor, dead-man switch, and pre-authorized runbook: the top ten bills, customer notification templates, who to call, how to pause automated agents and revoke tokens, and a wind-down-or-sell pack with a handoff to a route or book sale.
why_now: Owners increasingly hand credentials to AI agents and automations, and the 2026 loosening of SBA lending (7(a) plus 504 up to $10M) makes lenders care about key-person risk. The boomer owner cohort is aging.
revenue_model: $199 setup plus $19/month direct, wholesale at $99 per client to advisors, and API licensing to lenders.
non_obvious_insight: For the smallest businesses, succession usually means continuity, not sale. The distributor is the person who sells the life policy, who needs a reason to call every client each year.
first_30_days: Recruit five independent insurance agents or estate attorneys and offer white-label onboarding for 50 clients. Test whether successors can complete a simulated break-glass drill in under an hour.

title: Cell-Type-Restricted Promoters for Safer AAV
one_liner: AI-designed, primary-cell-validated regulatory sequences that switch AAV or LNP transgenes on only in target tissues and off in the liver.
customer: Gene therapy developers in muscle, heart and CNS (DMD, LGMD, cardiomyopathies) and capsid or CDMO companies wanting a detargeting cassette.
problem: High-dose systemic AAV caused acute liver failure deaths in 2025: three Sarepta patients, followed by a boxed warning and removal of non-ambulatory eligibility by Nov 14, 2025. Capsid engineering gets the attention, but the expression cassette is a second lever. Common promoters (CMV, CAG) are strong but non-specific, and miR-122 target sites only partly suppress liver expression.
solution: Generative design plus MPRA in iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and skeletal muscle cells and in primary human hepatocytes, ranking 10^4-10^5 sequences for high target and low liver expression. Deliver compact promoter-enhancer sets (under ~500 bp) with an optional miR-detargeting cassette, validated in vitro and in one partner rodent or NHP pilot.
why_now: The 2025 safety crisis is pushing dose reduction and liver detargeting. MPRA and generative sequence models are mature, DNA is cheap, and FDA's move toward human-relevant methods favors human primary-cell data.
revenue_model: $150-300k design-and-validation project plus a $50-200k license, with milestones or light royalties.
non_obvious_insight: The industry over-indexes on capsids, yet toxicity tracks where the transgene is expressed at dose. Compact regulatory parts are modular IP that stacks with any capsid, so one library serves many developers.
first_30_days: Run an MPRA on about 20k designed sequences in iPSC cardiomyocytes versus hepatocytes ($40-60k in reagents and sequencing). Publish a preprint and pitch 15 DMD, LGMD and cardiac programs on $50k pilots.

title: Camera-Free Certified: No-Record Spaces for Smart Glasses
one_liner: A certification, signage, staff-training and radio-detection service that lets gyms, spas, clinics and bars credibly promise 'no recording devices here' as camera glasses go mainstream.
customer: Owners of boutique gyms and pilates studios (especially women-focused), salons and spas, therapist and medical practices, schools, coworking spaces and event organizers. Their insurers are the eventual channel.
problem: Camera glasses look like ordinary eyewear. Researchers and journalists have documented men covertly filming women in gyms, workplaces and beaches. New York State courts banned them from all 1,240 courthouses in July 2026, and the Air Force, DEF CON 34 and UK Comic Con have banned them too. Yet as of July 2026 no major US gym chain had a formal smart-glasses policy, and staff have no acceptable way to check.
solution: Three tiers. (1) A policy kit with signage, member-agreement language and staff scripts ($29-49/month). (2) A 'Camera-Free Certified' badge with mystery audits, listed in a consumer directory of no-record places. (3) A discreet front-desk appliance or app that passively scans for the Bluetooth and Wi-Fi signals glasses emit and quietly alerts staff. Start with the kit and badge, and add detection once there are customers.
why_now: Smart-glasses sales climbed after Meta's Ray-Ban Display launch in late 2025. In 2026 scandals reached the mainstream, Meta bricked units with tampered recording LEDs, and institutions began banning them in a burst. Venue owners now face the liability question first.
revenue_model: $39-299 per month per venue by tier, plus one-time detection hardware, audit fees, and later insurer referral fees for certified venues.
non_obvious_insight: Bans fail without enforcement, and enforcement fails without a socially acceptable way to check. The moat is the certification norm, like 'smoke-free' or 'kosher', not the detector, which is a commodity. Women-only gyms and studios are the beachhead because 'safe to change here' is a direct marketing hook, and once one studio in a town is certified its competitors have to follow.
first_30_days: Ship the policy kit and printable signage in week one. Pitch 30 boutique studios, spas and therapist offices with a 'be the first certified venue in your city' offer. Aim for 10 paying at about $39/month. Build a Raspberry Pi or phone-based BLE scanning prototype with one pilot studio and launch a simple map of certified spaces.

title: Serial-Level Collateral Registry for GPU Lenders
one_liner: The independent field-exam firm and cross-lender double-pledge registry for AI hardware debt, built on the military rule that a serial number appears on one hand receipt only.
customer: Private-credit funds, banks, equipment lessors, ABS trustees and insurers financing neocloud GPU fleets, which now hold well over $20 billion in GPU-backed debt. Secondary: neoclouds that need audit-ready proof to borrow at lower spreads.
problem: Lenders rely on borrower-supplied serial lists, telemetry and occasional inspections. After the Tricolor and First Brands double-pledging scandals (the SEC charged Tricolor's former executives in August 2026), lenders know 'the same collateral pledged twice' is real. GPU servers sit in multi-tenant colocation halls, are easy to move, swap or re-pledge to another SPV, and telemetry can be spoofed. Serial-number UCC filings are rarely searched across lenders, and a colo technician paid by the borrower is not an independent counter.
solution: Three layers. (1) A repeatable two-person independent inventory protocol: witnessed reads of chassis label, BMC out-of-band serial and GPU-level serial, plus rack and cage photos, location and power draw. (2) Serialized tamper-evident seals on cages and rack doors, checked at each visit. (3) A privacy-preserving cross-lender registry of hashed serials so a lender learns whether a serial is already pledged elsewhere without revealing its book. Deliver monthly compliance packages that plug into the loan's reporting covenants for the trustee.
why_now: GPU-backed lending crossed $20 billion, and CoreWeave's $8.5 billion delayed-draw term loan (March 2026) showed the asset class reaching investment-grade structures. Tricolor and First Brands made 'verify the collateral independently' a board-level demand in private credit. Loan documents already grant lenders inspection rights, so the buyer has the access but not the in-house field-exam capability. Export-control diversion risk adds a second reason for chain-of-custody evidence.
revenue_model: Per-site audit of $15-50k, annual monitoring retainer of $50-250k per facility, registry subscriptions of $50-200k per lender, and trustee or insurer reporting packages. Long-term, per-basis-point fees on financed collateral under verification.
non_obvious_insight: Fraud lives at the seam between paper and physical, and the only reliable control is a count by someone who does not report to the borrower. That is what a military property book officer and a sensitive-item inventory do. Lenders will not share collateral lists with each other but will share hashes to avoid being second in line, so the registry becomes the moat. Telemetry proves a box is powered on, not that it is the box you financed.
first_30_days: Recruit 2-3 former property book or supply officers plus a data-center operations technician. Write and publish the audit protocol. Approach 5 mid-tier credit funds and equipment lenders (not the giants) that do GPU deals and lack field-exam staff. Offer a fixed-fee pilot audit on a live deal using the lender's existing inspection rights. Get a securities and privacy lawyer to bless the hashed-serial registry design before any lender data is pooled.

title: Voice-Agent Cash-Price Negotiator for Imaging
one_liner: AI voice agents that call 20-30 local facilities, negotiate a guaranteed cash bundle for an MRI, CT or scope, and book it for the newly uninsured.
customer: Uninsured and high-deductible patients (Urban estimates 4.8M newly uninsured after the ACA subsidy expiry; subsidy-cliff self-employed), small employers, and imaging centers, labs and ASCs with idle capacity.
problem: Posted prices are inconsistent and unusable, and cash prices for the same MRI can differ ~10x. Patients will not make 20 phone calls or negotiate, while facilities have idle slots.
solution: The patient submits an order. Agents call and email facilities for real quotes and slot availability, negotiate global-fee prepay bundles, filter for accreditation and quality, return one guaranteed price and book, with escrowed payment.
why_now: Real-time voice agents became reliable in 2025-26, and coverage loss is growing (ACA subsidies expired; Medicaid work requirements from Jan 2027). Posted-price marketplaces exist but they don't negotiate dynamically.
revenue_model: $19-39 per booked procedure plus a 5-10% fee from facilities filling otherwise idle slots (cash-pay only, structured to avoid federal-program referral issues).
non_obvious_insight: Cash price is a negotiated market for empty slots. Discovery cost used to be too high per patient, and voice agents make it nearly free.
first_30_days: Concierge 50 MRI, CT and colonoscopy quotes in one metro with call scripts and an LLM voice agent on top. Publish the price spread, sign 5 imaging centers, and charge $29 per booking.

title: Ex-Sales-Rep Route Collectives for Critical-Metal Scrap
one_liner: Commission-only teams of laid-off SDRs and inside-sales reps that each own a territory and sign machine shops and dental and electronics labs to take-back programs for tungsten carbide and cobalt scrap. Lots are aggregated and sold directly to domestic reclaimers.
customer: Sellers: tens of thousands of small generators such as machine and tool-and-die shops, carbide grinding shops and dental labs. Buyers: domestic carbide and tungsten reclaimers and refiners that now need US-allocated feedstock. Reps: displaced sales staff.
problem: The BIS rule restricts tungsten scrap exports and the DoD and DOE are subsidizing domestic supply, but supply is scattered across small generators who sell to local yards at a steep discount or trash the hard-to-value streams such as grinding swarf. The bottleneck is sales coverage of the long tail, not recovery technology. Entry-level SDR and BDR roles are among the first white-collar jobs AI is absorbing, leaving a large pool of trained cold-outreach talent.
solution: Each rep owns a metro territory and signs 30-100 shops to a free take-back program: lockable bins, an assay or XRF-based price sheet, payment by lot and simple compliance paperwork (including BIS and toll-processing documentation). Consolidate through partner yards or carriers and sell aggregated lots to reclaimers on term offtake. Start with carbide inserts and grinding swarf, then add cobalt-alloy turnings. Reps keep 15-25% of the net spread and a software backbone handles pricing, pickup scheduling and payouts.
why_now: The BIS allocation rule created a domestic-first buyer set. Machine shops are squeezed by tariffs and input costs and welcome found cash. SDR and entry-level sales roles are being cut in 2026 and reps are actively looking for commission work. The DOE ($134M) and DoD rare-earth and critical-mineral funding raise buyers' willingness to pay for documented domestic feed.
revenue_model: Spread on aggregated lots (buy at a fixed percentage of the reclaimer price and sell at the offtake price). Service fee on compliance paperwork. Later, SaaS for yards and reclaimers.
non_obvious_insight: In critical-material recycling the scarce resource is neither collection technology nor recovery chemistry but sales coverage of thousands of tiny generators. The people best at long-tail coverage are exactly the ones AI has just made cheap.
first_30_days: Pick one machine-shop-dense metro. Get a reclaimer to sign an offtake letter. Recruit five ex-SDRs and have them call 500 shops from public industrial directories. Collect and sell the first few tons of carbide and swarf, and document real price gaps versus the shops' current yards.

title: Cross-Landlord Fake-Employer and Fake-Reference Registry
one_liner: A shared network that spots rental fraud by the out-of-band details forgers cannot fake, such as the same 'HR' phone number, burner line or 'previous landlord' reused across dozens of leasing offices.
customer: Independent and mid-size property managers (50 to 5,000 units) who process applications themselves and lack a fraud team. They pay per application or per portfolio. Later customers are auto lenders, buy-here-pay-here dealers, gig-work platforms and small-balance mortgage lenders, who all verify employers and references the same way.
problem: Application fraud is now professional. The pay stubs, bank statements and offer letters are fabricated, and the 'employer' is a shell whose 'HR line' is answered by an accomplice. Even the 'previous landlord' reference is a friend. Every leasing office catches one of these files, throws it out, and never tells anyone. The same ring then applies at the property across town and eventually gets a lease. The eviction that follows costs $8,000 to $20,000 and several months. Document-forensics tools catch sloppy Photoshop, but once image generators can produce perfect pay stubs (as they now can), the lie is no longer in the PDF. It is in the phone number and the employer that do not exist.
solution: An API and browser extension for leasing staff. Staff enter the employer name, HR phone or email, the previous-landlord contact and the stated address. The system returns a risk read built from three signals. First, telecom line-type and age (VoIP or burner, number recently ported or activated). Second, business-registry and domain checks (EIN, formation date, mismatched address, brand-new domain). Third, and this is the moat, network signals: how many distinct applicants at how many unrelated landlords used this exact phone, email, employer or landlord reference in the last 12 months, and whether any of those files were confirmed fraud by a participating PM. Participants contribute confirmed-fraud entities and get read access, and entries link to entities (phones, domains, businesses), not to named individuals. That design keeps most of the data outside consumer-report regulation, and any person-linked entry gets a dispute and correction workflow.
why_now: Generative image models make forged financial documents indistinguishable in 2025 and 2026, which pushes the defensive signal from document pixels to out-of-band verification. Fraud-detection vendors for leasing are consolidating around documents, so an entity-level shared registry sits in the gap. Large PMs have internal fraud teams, and the long tail of independents has nothing. Rental markets that are softer with more concessions also attract more fraud-ring activity aimed at free-rent giveaways and quick move-ins.
revenue_model: $1.50 to $3.00 per application check, or $149 to $499 per month by portfolio size with a contribution-based discount. Enterprise API licensing to lenders and platforms later. Data-contribution credits make the network self-seeding.
non_obvious_insight: Rental fraud rings reuse infrastructure across landlords far more than they reuse identities. The same 'HR' number answers for 14 different companies. But no single landlord sees more than one or two, so the pattern is invisible without a network. It works like ISO ClaimSearch did for insurance claims. Because the registry tracks entities and not people, it sidesteps most of the fair-lending and consumer-reporting objections that killed earlier landlord blacklists.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 PMs from local NARPM chapters and landlord Facebook groups. Ask each to send the last 20 to 50 confirmed-fraud files (phone, email, employer, reference only, no SSNs), and seed the database from those. Run the pooled data for overlaps and show each PM how many of their 'unique' fraudsters overlapped with someone else's. Ship a Chrome extension that checks a phone or email against the database plus Twilio Lookup. Free for the first 60 days for contributors, then $149 per month. Have a fair-credit-reporting attorney review the entity-only design and the dispute process before charging.

title: Shared-Docket Lawsuits Against Scam Infrastructure
one_liner: Turn Google's and Microsoft's civil-seizure playbook into a membership where 20-50 mid-size banks and brands co-file one John Doe action against the kit or ring impersonating all of them.
customer: Regional banks, credit unions, toll and payment operators, and mid-market retail and logistics brands that are repeatedly impersonated. They are too small to fund a $1M lawsuit alone.
problem: Takedown notices are whack-a-mole. Criminal enforcement takes years, and the FBI is warning about $1.6B+ in law-enforcement impersonation alone. Phishing kits sell for about $50, and one E-ZPass smishing ring sent 330,000 texts a day and took about $1B over 3 years. Big Tech gets ex parte orders to seize domains and servers, but mid-size victims are left with abuse reports.
solution: An evidence-and-litigation-ops company paired with an independent law firm (fees billed separately, to respect fee-splitting rules). It continuously builds dossiers on the kits hitting its members and drafts one multi-plaintiff John Doe complaint (Lanham Act, CFAA, RICO where apt). It then obtains TRO and preliminary-injunction orders that compel registrars, registries, hosts, CDNs, and stablecoin issuers to act. Members pay a retainer plus a per-seizure fee and receive the takedown results.
why_now: Google's 2025 suit against the operators of the Lighthouse smishing kit and Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit seizures created templates and precedents. Kits are centralized, so one order can protect hundreds of brands. The US-UK agreement to coordinate scam-center takedowns (Sep 4 2026) signals political tailwind for civil action.
revenue_model: $2-5K per month per member. 30 members is roughly $1M ARR. Success fees per seized infrastructure cluster. Legal costs passed through.
non_obvious_insight: Litigation cost scales with the number of defendant networks, not the number of victims, so it works like a reverse class action: fixed cost, split N ways. Kit concentration means a single order hits infrastructure serving hundreds of brands. Everyone assumes only Microsoft and Google can afford this, and nobody sells it as a shared product.
first_30_days: Retain a boutique IP/cyber litigation firm. Recruit 5 founding members through a credit-union league or toll-operator association. Deliver each an evidence dossier on the kit currently hitting them. Pre-sell $2K/month founding memberships to fund the first filing within about 90 days.

title: Low-Background Human Data: Witnessed Creative Corpora
one_liner: Like pre-war steel, certifiably human creative work is becoming scarce, so sell fresh, witnessed, process-verified corpora to labs and detector vendors.
customer: AI labs and evaluation teams, detector vendors that need gold human test sets, and data-licensing brokers.
problem: Anything scraped from the web after 2023 is contaminated (AI is over 50% of Deezer daily uploads, and large shares of text are machine-made). Labs need uncontaminated creative data for evals, style diversity and fine-tuning. Detector vendors need known-human sets to measure false positives. No one can currently prove any given item is human.
solution: A paid panel of ID-verified writers, illustrators and musicians produce work under witnessed capture (screen and keystroke logs, DAW session logs, timelapse). Each item ships with process evidence in a quarterly dataset subscription. Creators are paid per item plus royalties from dataset revenue. Start with a 5,000-item 'human baseline' across text, illustration and music.
why_now: Contamination is now measurable, detector-scoring consequences are public, and human data has become a large market. Process-capture tooling for creative apps is cheap.
revenue_model: $25-300k per dataset subscription, per-item pricing of $5-200, and evaluation-as-a-service, with 50-60% of revenue to creators.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce good is not more data but certifiably unpolluted data, and every improvement in AI raises its price. The premium for 'guaranteed human' is set by buyers who cannot get it anywhere else.
first_30_days: Recruit 100 creators from paid-newsletter and Discord communities. Build a capture app (browser extension plus DAW logging). Send a sample data card to detector vendors and two labs' eval teams, and sell a $25-75k baseline set.

title: Impersonation Firewall at the Distributor Gate
one_liner: A KYC-style API that distributors call before publishing a release under an existing artist name, so one upstream check protects every streaming service at once.
customer: Mid-size self-serve music distributors and label-service companies, which carry the upload volume, the DSP penalties and the legal heat from labels. Estates and small catalogs benefit downstream.
problem: Everyone treats DSP-side approval as the fix, such as Spotify's Artist Profile Protection beta (Mar 24, 2026) and its verified badges (Apr 30). But impersonation enters through distributors, which sit upstream of every DSP. The brief cites Sony's 135,000+ removal requests, and AI tracks were pushed onto pages of Jeff Tweedy, Father John Misty and the late Blaze Foley in Aug 2025. Spotify's protection only helps artists who opt in, on one service.
solution: An API that scores each new release in seconds. It checks (1) name and identifier collisions against existing artist pages on public DSP APIs, (2) proof of control over the claimed identity through handle-linking challenges and a short liveness video for unknown names, and (3) audio-embedding similarity between the new master and the claimed artist's catalog. Suspicious releases go to a human review queue with an evidence pack. It returns allow, hold or reject, and every decision is logged.
why_now: Platform policing arrived (Spotify beta, TIDAL, Bandcamp) but only at the shelf, not the door. Deezer reports AI above 50% of uploads, so distributors face rising takedown and fine volume. AI-powered impersonation is now cheap.
revenue_model: $0.10-0.40 per release check with a $1-3k/month minimum, plus review-queue seats and a premium tier for auto-holding high-risk releases.
non_obvious_insight: The platforms sell AI tools themselves and each protects only its own pages. The distributor is the only place where cost, liability and the payout relationship line up, and a KYC check there is cheap compared with cleanup after upload.
first_30_days: Build a prototype on public Spotify, Deezer and Apple search APIs plus open audio embeddings. Back-test it on the documented impersonation cases. Offer 10 mid-size distributors a free retro-audit of their last 90 days of releases, and convert one or two into a paid pilot.

title: Abandoned Property and Tenant-Death Response Crew
one_liner: A per-event service that handles the legally dangerous moments landlords dread most, such as a tenant who vanishes leaving belongings or a tenant who dies alone, with statutory clocks, next-of-kin outreach and documented disposal.
customer: Property managers and small landlords, who pay per event ($400 to $1,500). Later customers are eldercare social workers, hospital discharge teams, medical examiners' offices and estate attorneys, who all need someone to close out a residence properly.
problem: A 400-unit manager deals with a handful of abandonments a year and one to three tenant deaths. Each event is handled ad hoc. Abandoned-property statutes vary by state, with notice periods, itemized inventory rules, value thresholds and sale-or-storage requirements. One mistake, such as tossing a bin or entering too early, creates conversion or wrongful-eviction liability. With a death, no one has authority to enter or dispose of belongings, the estate has no representative yet, next of kin are unknown or hostile, rent accrues, and the unit sits dark for months. Hoarding and biohazard situations make it worse. There is no standard vendor, so the maintenance supervisor is doing legal and emotional work no one trained him for.
solution: A regional response team with a state-specific statutory workflow. Step one is intake and legal-clock software, which starts the required notice dates, produces the notices, photo-inventory and valuation report and stores it as evidence. Step two is next-of-kin and estate-representative outreach, with sensitivity training for the caller. Step three is secure storage in a partner facility, then sale, donation or disposal exactly as the statute allows, with receipts. Step four is coordinating hoarding or biohazard remediation and the final walk-through for deposit accounting. A companion product is an e-signable lease addendum letting tenants (especially seniors) name an emergency contact and authorized person for post-death property disposition, in the states where that is permitted. That builds a pipeline of pre-authorized cases and makes each later event simple.
why_now: The number of renters aged 65+ living alone is growing fast, which means more deaths in rental units and more hoarding and welfare issues. Several states have recently added or modernized tenant-designated-contact and abandoned-property procedures, though rules remain patchy. Software-only proptech has ignored this because it is field work. Junk-removal and storage marketplaces have made the physical logistics cheap to subcontract.
revenue_model: $400 to $1,500 flat fee per abandonment or death event, plus pass-through storage and disposal cost at a 15 to 25% markup. Optional readiness subscription ($1 to $2 per unit per month) for PMs, covering the lease addendum, templates and priority response. Eldercare and estate-attorney referral relationships add a second channel.
non_obvious_insight: Ordinary landlords fear the eviction. Experienced managers fear the abandonment and the death, because the law in those cases punishes shortcuts, no procedure exists, and the loss (months of rent plus liability) is bigger than a normal eviction. Nobody sells the service because each case is small and the required knowledge is a stack of 50 state statutes. That fragmentation is the moat: once you have playbooks for a handful of states, competitors cannot copy them quickly.
first_30_days: Pick one state and read the abandoned-property and death-of-tenant statutes closely, ideally with a landlord-tenant attorney on a fixed-fee review. Build the notice, inventory and timeline templates. Sign three PMs (find them through the local NARPM or apartment association) to a pilot: 'call us on the next event, first one at cost'. Line up a junk-removal company, a storage unit partner and a biohazard remediation subcontractor. Publish a simple blog page and a landlord-association talk titled 'What to do when a tenant dies or disappears' to start inbound.

title: Enclave Escrow: Buy Data by Measured Lift
one_liner: A confidential-compute clean room where the buyer's evaluation runs on the seller's data inside an attested enclave, and the price is set by the measured lift, so neither side reveals its asset before agreeing.
customer: Quant funds, ML teams and R&D groups buying alternative or proprietary datasets, and the small data sellers (satellite counts, AIS ship data, web panels, lab datasets) who cannot afford NDAs and legal cycles. Autonomous buyer agents are the growth channel.
problem: Arrow's information paradox: you cannot value data without seeing it, but once you see it you do not need to buy it. Sellers therefore refuse trials or overprice, buyers waste budget on blind purchases, and agents purchasing autonomously cannot sign NDAs or judge value.
solution: Seller uploads an encrypted dataset. Buyer uploads a hashed evaluation harness (a backtest, a fine-tune validation run, an accuracy test). Both run inside a CPU plus GPU trusted execution environment with remote attestation. Only a signed lift score leaves the enclave, under a per-pair query budget or differential-privacy noise to stop the score being used as an extraction oracle. A pre-agreed schedule converts lift into a license price, and payment triggers automatically if the buyer opts in.
why_now: Confidential computing on Hopper and Blackwell GPUs now runs with little performance penalty and produces GPU-signed attestation reports. Cloud providers and GPU-TEE clouds sell it off the shelf. Agents with pay-per-request data endpoints are starting to buy data blind.
revenue_model: 5-10% of transaction value, compute pass-through, $5-25k per paid evaluation for funds, and a subscription for private clean rooms.
non_obvious_insight: Sell the measurement, not the data. The thing placed in escrow is an experiment both sides commit to before seeing the result, which turns the sale into outcome-linked pricing and lets tiny sellers with no legal team participate. Bounding the lift oracle (query budgets) is the hard, defensible engineering piece.
first_30_days: Sign 3 small alt-data sellers and 2 small funds or ML teams for paid pilots. Use rented confidential VMs and a manually built harness for each evaluation. Charge $5k per evaluation and deliver a signed report. Use results to write a public 'pay for lift' pricing template.

title: Hotel-Signed Days-in-Country Proofs for Remote Teams
one_liner: Hotels and co-living spaces issue signed, privacy-minimal 'nights in this country' attestations, so employers can prove where remote staff worked without tracking their phones.
customer: Finance, tax or mobility leads at remote-first companies of 30-500 staff that run 'work from anywhere' weeks. Secondary payers are co-living operators and boutique hotels that want a 'workation-verified' badge.
problem: A few weeks abroad can create payroll, social-security and permanent-establishment exposure, and employers need day counts to defend their position. In the EU, GPS or phone tracking of staff is legally toxic (GDPR proportionality, works councils), so companies rely on self-reported spreadsheets. The EU Entry/Exit System has logged border crossings automatically since April 2026, yet neither traveler nor employer gets that data in a usable form. 40+ nomad-visa regimes each have different thresholds.
solution: A thin layer on top of hotel and co-living check-in. At checkout the guest opts in, and the property issues a signed attestation (country, region, date range, licence ID, guest name and nothing else) into the traveler's wallet. The employer's HR or tax tool ingests it by CSV or API, and a country rules pack warns when a threshold is near. The MVP needs no integration: a web form, a signed PDF with a QR code, and a shared ledger template.
why_now: EES has been fully live since 10 Apr 2026, so stays are now machine-tracked at the border but invisible to employers. ETIAS slipping to 2027 keeps the friction alive. Hybrid and workation policies have matured, and 40+ nomad visas make cross-border patchwork the norm.
revenue_model: The employer pays about $6 per attestation or $10 per employee per year for the ledger and rules pack. The property pays about $49 a month for a verified listing in a 'workation-ready' directory. Tax advisers can resell it.
non_obvious_insight: Employers cannot lawfully surveil location, but hospitality already produces third-party presence records by law (guest registration and folios). The missing piece is a consent-based export, so the evidence sits in the hotel and not on the phone.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 co-living spaces and boutique hotels (Lisbon, Canaries, Split, Tbilisi) through operator communities. Have one cross-border tax adviser review a one-page attestation spec. Issue attestations by hand. Pitch 5 remote-first startups through their payroll and tax advisers at a $500 pilot, and count first revenue when the first ledger is delivered.

title: CRA Continuity Kit for One-Person Vendors
one_liner: An outsourced EU Cyber Resilience Act desk that handles the 24h/72h/14-day vulnerability reporting clock and keeps a signed 10-year release vault with a dead-man's-switch escrow, built for micro-vendors with no security team.
customer: Solo and micro hardware, firmware, app and SaaS vendors that sell into the EU, such as ESP32 and Raspberry Pi based device makers on Tindie or Crowd Supply, small GmbHs, and indie app publishers. There is no size exemption. They pay EUR 79-399/month per product.
problem: CRA Article 14 reporting began 11 September 2026: a 24-hour early warning, a 72-hour notification and a 14-day final report via ENISA's Single Reporting Platform, with fines up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover. A one-person German GmbH selling firmware asks how to comply given CE marking, a technical file, 'every security update you ship has to stay available for 10 years' and no size threshold. Maintainers are already bailing out: the croniter fork was archived citing the CRA.
solution: A subscription that provides (1) a named on-call reporting desk that prepares and files the early warning, notification and final report on the vendor's delegated authority against a pre-agreed playbook; (2) SBOM generation and continuous vulnerability watch tied to the customer's release artifacts, to detect an 'actively exploited' trigger; (3) an immutable, signed release vault holding every shipped update for 10+ years, with a dead-man's-switch: if the vendor stops responding or dissolves, the firmware source and update artifacts are released to customers or a nominated steward; (4) a fixed-price 'CRA readiness sprint' that produces the technical-file skeleton and declaration-of-conformity scaffolding.
why_now: The reporting obligation went live 11 September 2026, so this is a forced-spend deadline, not a forecast. Full obligations follow in December 2027. Legal commentators say many still associate the CRA only with consumer IoT and are unprepared.
revenue_model: EUR 1,500 fixed-price readiness sprint, then EUR 79-399/month per product for the reporting retainer and vault, tiered by product count and risk class. Optional per-incident filing fee. Channel deals with device marketplaces and Linux/embedded distributors.
non_obvious_insight: The gap is not compliance dashboards (the Ask HN thread already lists Vulert, ReARM and the ORC WG hub) but staffed responsiveness and durable custody: a solo founder cannot staff a 24-hour clock or credibly promise 10 years of availability. A dead-man's-switch vault turns the founder's bus-factor into a compliance asset. Escrow at end of life is a recurring HN demand, e.g. 'When you release a product, you should be required to put the source code in escrow, so it can be released at EoL' https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44531176, and vendors ask for escrow tooling https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46402528. Evidence of demand: one-person GmbH asking for help https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49520688; obligations and fines https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/09/11/eus-cyber-resilience-act-starts-the-24-hour-vulnerability-clock/5295821; croniter archived https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=43168860.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 design partners from the Open Regulatory Compliance WG CRA hub, Torizon CRA summit attendees, and Tindie/Crowd Supply sellers, plus the author of the Ask HN thread. Sell the EUR 1,500 sprint with a written 24h playbook and SBOM pipeline for their repos. Stand up the vault on object-lock storage with signed manifests and a heartbeat check-in. Have a CRA-literate lawyer review the delegation-of-filing template. Convert sprint customers to the retainer.

title: Benefits Administrator for Pet-Care Subsidies
one_liner: When hundreds of millions in philanthropy and city funds must reach the right households through thousands of small clinics, someone needs the HSA-administrator equivalent: eligibility, vouchers, payment and audit.
customer: Foundation grantees and programs (Duffield and PetSmart Charities recipients), county animal services and spay-neuter voucher programs. Clinics are the redemption side.
problem: Duffield committed $250M over 5 years, starting with 250 grants of $10K plus $10M in multi-year awards. Grantees run eligibility by paper forms and spreadsheets, clinics wait weeks for reimbursement, funders cannot compare cost per pet outcome, and fraud and overhead eat funds.
solution: Verify proxy eligibility (SNAP, Medicaid, housing-voucher documents or benefit APIs), issue capped QR or card vouchers by procedure category, pay clinics within 5 business days, and export standardized reporting (pets treated, cost, outcome, declined) to funders. Define a shared outcome taxonomy that becomes the field standard.
why_now: The $250M Duffield commitment (2026-09-17) and PetSmart Charities' $100M created hundreds of new grantees at once. Card-issuing and instant-payout APIs let a small team run a closed-loop voucher program.
revenue_model: 4-7% administration fee on disbursed dollars (funded from grant overhead lines), SaaS fee per grantee, and data and reporting subscriptions for funders.
non_obvious_insight: Money is not the binding constraint; distribution rails are. Human benefit administrators (HSA and EBT processors) became large businesses because funders needed accountability. About 250 first-round grantees have no back office, so the standard-setter for outcomes measurement owns the funders' reporting.
first_30_days: Contact 20 first-round grantees and 5 county animal services. Offer a free voucher tool to one program with a $10K grant, run through 3 clinics, and publish an outcomes one-pager. Then brief funder program officers on standardized reporting.

title: Camera-to-Courtroom Evidence Provenance for Small Firms
one_liner: A capture app and export service that timestamps and cryptographically signs photos, video, texts and voicemails at collection, packaged with an authentication affidavit for court.
customer: Family-law, employment, landlord-tenant and personal-injury firms with up to 10 attorneys, their clients, legal-aid groups and HR investigators.
problem: Deepfakes make every screenshot and clip attackable. Courts and rule-makers are debating standards for machine-generated and possibly fabricated evidence (background, verify), and opposing counsel increasingly says 'that could be AI'. Honest clients then need a forensic expert at thousands of dollars per item to prove authenticity.
solution: Mobile capture that uses C2PA Content Credentials where phones support them (Pixel 10 added camera-level signing in 2025, background, verify) with a fallback for other devices, an SMS, WhatsApp and iMessage exporter with hash chaining, RFC 3161 trusted timestamps, chain-of-custody logs, and a one-click authentication package with a declaration template and a verifier page for the court. Optional expert-declaration add-on.
why_now: Mainstream phones gained hardware-backed provenance in 2025, judicial scrutiny of AI-generated evidence rose through 2025-26, and timestamping and signing infrastructure is now near-free.
revenue_model: $9-29 per case pack, $99-299/month per firm, and $250-500 per expert add-on.
non_obvious_insight: The generative-AI problem for law is not only fake evidence getting in, but real evidence being dismissed. Provenance at creation is a right-of-reply tool for the party with fewer resources, so the customer is the weaker litigant's lawyer.
first_30_days: Ship the capture app and message exporter, pilot with 15 family-law solos, get a forensic examiner to co-sign the package and stage a mock authentication hearing with a law-school clinic. Charge $99/month afterward.

title: UL for Talking Toys: Behavioral Safety Lab
one_liner: An independent lab that red-teams AI toys and kid-facing companion gadgets with child personas, then sells scorecards and a 'passed' seal to brands and retailers.
customer: AI-toy brands and ODMs launching in the US, licensors of kids' IP, and big-box and online retailers' product-safety and legal teams, plus toy-industry insurers.
problem: Physical toy labs test lead and choking hazards but nobody tests what a toy says across a 200-turn conversation, whether guardrails drift, where audio goes, or whether privacy claims are true. Late-2025 consumer testing reportedly found AI toys giving inappropriate content (not verified in the brief). Retailers carry the liability, and the FTC's 6(b) inquiry, SB 243 and the amended COPPA rule raise the stakes.
solution: A standard suite of about 300 child-persona conversations (ages 4-12, varied accents), child-style jailbreak probing, sensitive-topic sweeps, long-horizon persona drift, network capture of data flows and retention, and verification of COPPA claims. Deliverables are a scorecard, fix list, re-test and a versioned seal retailers can require.
why_now: Holiday 2026 is the first mass AI-toy season (Mattel-OpenAI partnership, from memory; Character.AI's under-18 exit), and retailers' legal teams need evidence by Q4. The buying window is right now.
revenue_model: $12-40k per product per version, annual retainers for brands, and seal licensing fees.
non_obvious_insight: Retailers, not parents, are the choke point, and they buy assurance rather than products. The test is dynamic (behavior over time) rather than static (materials), which makes it a new category of lab created by regulators' fear.
first_30_days: Buy 10 AI toys and gadgets (about $1.5k) and publish a public holiday AI-toy behavior report with methodology. Send private reports to 5 retailer compliance heads and 10 brands. Offer paid re-tests to any brand that fails.

title: Batteries That Pay Off Utility Arrears
one_liner: Install free home batteries in households behind on bills and let capacity payments retire the debt, which is cheaper for the utility than writing it off.
customer: Utilities, co-ops and munis in high-capacity-price regions (PJM first) that run arrears and shutoff programs. State PUCs and community action agencies co-sponsor. The utility pays from bad-debt and program budgets.
problem: 13.4M households were disconnected in 2024 and about 1 in 6 are behind on bills. Rates rose 7.3% in a year and this is a midterm issue. At the $325/MW-day cap, each kW of dispatchable capacity is worth about $118 a year, so a 5 kW home battery is worth roughly $590 a year gross, before accreditation haircuts and the aggregator's share.
solution: A no-cost 10 kWh 'bill-relief battery' for arrears households, enrolled in a utility or aggregator capacity program. Capacity and energy revenue is credited against the arrears balance for 5-7 years, after which the customer keeps it or the utility retains it. The company handles installation, financing and dispatch. The utility gets less bad debt and fewer politically toxic shutoffs.
why_now: Capacity prices hit the cap, packs cost about $70/kWh, dispatch at scale is proven, and utilities are under political pressure on affordability with few tools.
revenue_model: Per-install fee, a share of capacity revenue while the arrears are being retired, utility program payments, and project finance spread.
non_obvious_insight: At this capacity price, a battery earns more than it costs to give one away. Utility bad debt is a hidden capex budget that has never been spent on assets.
first_30_days: Get one utility's arrears distribution and model unit economics under current capacity prices. Pitch five community action agencies and three co-ops or munis on a 50-home pilot funded by weatherization-adjacent money. Line up a philanthropic first-loss guarantee.

title: Supplier Divorce Protection: Tool Census and Overrun Forensics
one_liner: When a US manufacturer leaves a Chinese contract manufacturer, we find out which molds and dies it really owns, and prove whether the ex-supplier is still running them off the books.
customer: US OEMs and PE-owned manufacturers ($50M-$500M revenue) that moved or are moving injection-molded, die-cast, stamped or extruded product out of China within the last 24 months, and hold $200k-$5M of tooling there. The buyer is the COO or VP Supply Chain, with General Counsel as co-signer. General counsel and brand-protection managers are the second buyer.
problem: Most small and mid-size OEMs cannot say which tools they own, where they physically sit, or what condition they are in. The paper trail is a PO line item from 2016 and a WeChat thread. When the relationship ends, the supplier slow-walks tool release, demands storage or release fees, and sometimes runs overruns on your tooling on a third shift and sells them to distributors and marketplaces at a discount. You then compete against your own product, and lawyers cannot help because nobody can prove which tool made which part.
solution: Three stacked products. (1) Tool Census: a local partner audits each supplier on video and in person, laser-tags every tool with a serial, records its condition and appraised value, and captures a macro-photo 'fingerprint' library of each cavity (gate vestige, ejector-pin witness marks, texture flaws, parting-line signature). (2) Overrun Watch: monitor Amazon, Alibaba, 1688, Temu, eBay and Walmart Marketplace for look-alike parts, buy samples, and match them to cavity fingerprints, date wheels and lot codes with computer-vision-assisted forensics. That yields evidence packs for marketplace takedowns, CBP IPR recordation, or counsel. (3) Tool Extraction: negotiate release, handle Chinese export paperwork and freight, and re-qualify the tool in Ohio.
why_now: The Reshoring Initiative's 2026 survey shows 36% of OEMs reshored this year, up from 29%. The 2025 tariff whiplash ended a lot of Chinese supplier relationships, and the Feb 2026 Supreme Court IEEPA ruling is now churning sourcing decisions again, so the number of messy breakups is at a peak. Cheap macro-imaging and vision models make tool-mark matching, previously an expensive forensic-lab exercise, feasible at SMB prices.
revenue_model: Tool Census at $6k-$15k per supplier site. Overrun Watch at $2k-$5k per month per product family. Forensic evidence pack at $3k-$8k per case. Extraction at 8-12% of appraised tool value plus pass-through freight. Expected first-year ACV per client is $40k-$120k.
non_obvious_insight: Outsiders think IP loss in China means someone copies your design. Insiders know the far bigger leak is your own paid-for tool running unrecorded shifts, and that every cavity is a physical fingerprint the supplier cannot deny. Ownership of the tooling is the real leverage in any break-up, and almost nobody documents it until the day they need it.
first_30_days: Skip China operations at first. Sell a remote $2,500 'Marketplace Overrun Audit': buy 10 units of the client's product from 1688, Alibaba and Temu, compare them to the golden sample and lot codes, and deliver a one-page verdict. Sign 3 design partners through Ohio plant-manager and Reshoring Initiative networks, and line up a Dongguan or Ningbo audit contractor by referral. Book a one-hour consult with an IP litigator who will white-label the evidence-pack format.

title: Licensed Local-Language Speech Data Exchange
one_liner: Pay radio stations and call centers for rights-cleared audio and resell it to the voice-AI builders who cannot get it anywhere else.
customer: Voice-AI startups and model labs that need low-resource African and Indian language audio; radio stations and telco call centers are the suppliers.
problem: Foreign APIs are unusable for local voice because of latency and jitter. Startups like AethexAI train small models on call-center recordings and radio audio, but rights, cleaning and transcription are ad hoc.
solution: A consented, speaker-anonymised and transcribed archive with clear licences and revenue share for stations. The wedge is 3-5 stations in one language (Hausa, Yoruba or Swahili), with a sample set for a paying pilot.
why_now: 300M-1.7B parameter voice models now work in production, and Intron covers 57 languages. Labs face scrutiny over scraped data, and Sarvam and AethexAI are raising money.
revenue_model: $20-80 per cleaned, licensed hour, with 40-50% shared with the station, plus annual subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders assume low-resource data is unsellable because the markets are poor. The buyers are well-funded labs, and rights-cleared audio, not raw audio, is the bottleneck.
first_30_days: Sign three stations, digitise about 2,000 hours and clean 200 as a sample. Sell a paid pilot dataset to one voice-AI startup.

title: Recorded Parent Voices, Endowed to Outlive Us
one_liner: Guided, human-only voice and video milestone messages for the children of dying parents, with the hosting prepaid so the recordings outlive the company.
customer: Terminally ill parents of minor children, or their spouses. Referrals come from oncology and young-adult cancer social workers, child-life specialists, and hospice social workers. Hospice foundations sponsor families who cannot pay.
problem: Dying parents of young children want to leave their actual voice for the 16th birthday, the wedding and the first heartbreak. They start too late. By the time hospice admission happens, many patients are too sedated, breathless or confused to record anything usable. The generic tools (StoryWorth-style prompts, phone voice memos) produce rambling, prompt-less files. Families also do not trust vendors to still exist in 20 years. Meanwhile AI voice-cloning 'deadbots' are being pitched at the same families, and most of them recoil.
solution: A two-session guided capture (in person or on video) run by a trained 'legacy guide' with a chaplain or child-bereavement background. It uses a prompt library organized by the child's future age: what a 12-year-old needs to hear versus a 30-year-old. Examples: 'how I met your dad', 'what I was afraid of', 'what I'd say when you're furious at me', and a mundane category (how I laughed, my opinion of your first crush) that grown children say matters most. The output is edited, human-only audio and video with a strict no-synthesis policy. Each message is tagged to a milestone and delivered by the surviving guardian's app. There is a physical archival copy and printed transcripts. Hosting is prepaid into a trust-held reserve, with a contractual right to export everything if the company dies. Durability and authenticity are the product, not features.
why_now: AI voice-cloning is now cheap and good enough that grief-tech is being flooded with synthetic 'talk to your dead mom' products. Public and clinical unease about them is rising, which opens a clear 'only what they actually said' position. At least some early digital-afterlife vendors have folded or pivoted, so buyers are primed to ask 'will this exist in 2045?'. Phone-quality recording is now good enough that no studio is needed. I could not verify specific vendor failures in this session, so confirm before using them in marketing.
revenue_model: Roughly $450 for guided capture plus a one-time $600 to $900 permanence endowment (about $1,000 to $1,400 per family). The endowment funds 30-year hosting, and the reserve is held in a trust or escrow. Add-ons: printed keepsake book, extra milestone messages, and an 'audio blessing' set for each child. Hospice and hospital foundations sponsor uninsured families at a discounted wholesale rate.
non_obvious_insight: The market timing is wrong in everyone's mind. The recording window closes weeks before hospice, so the referral source is oncology, not hospice. What dying parents fear most is not death but vanishing, and that includes the file vanishing. Buyers will pay more for a credible 'this outlives our company' promise than for any feature. Refusing to synthesize is a selling point that families and chaplains will repeat.
first_30_days: Recruit two oncology or child-life social workers as design partners. Run 8 to 10 free pilot sessions using a phone and a $60 lavalier mic, and write the age-banded prompt library from what the kids' guardians say they'd want. Get a small-estates attorney or trust company to set up the escrow and export-if-we-fail clause. Put up a one-page site, then charge from case 11. Ask the first families for a written testimonial and referrals to two other oncology units.

title: Keep-the-House Buyout Desk for Divorcing Spouses
one_liner: A divorce-specific mortgage desk that keeps the low-rate first mortgage alive, gets the leaving spouse released, and funds the equity buyout with a small second lien instead of a full high-rate cash-out refinance.
customer: Divorcing homeowners, mostly aged 40 to 65, who want to keep the house. Channels: mediators, divorce attorneys, CDFAs and DIY-divorce platforms.
problem: A divorce decree cannot release a co-borrower from the mortgage. Only a formal assumption with release, which requires servicer underwriting of the keeping spouse, or a refinance can do that. Many conventional loans are not assumable, though a transfer to a spouse under a decree is exempt from due-on-sale, while FHA, VA and USDA loans can be assumed. Servicers often mishandle these requests. Many homeowners hold first mortgages far below today's rates, so a full refinance wrecks affordability and the house gets sold.
solution: Intake on loan type, rate, equity and incomes, then a one-page keep versus sell versus refinance model showing blended-rate math. Then execute the sequence: title transfer under the divorce exemption, an assumption-with-release packet built for the servicer, buyout financing through a partner HELOC or closed-end second lien (or a shared-equity note from the leaving spouse), and suggested decree language for attorneys, such as a buyout-financing contingency and a release deadline.
why_now: Millions of borrowers still hold sub-4% mortgages while current rates are higher, and tappable home equity is large. The share of divorces involving people over 50 keeps growing, and those couples have the most equity. DIY-divorce platforms now produce decrees with no mortgage plan.
revenue_model: A flat $495 to $995 planning fee. Broker compensation of about 1% to 2% on second-lien or HELOC originations (requires an NMLS-licensed loan officer or partner). Licensing to DIY-divorce platforms and mediation firms. Avoid referral fees to attorneys because of fee-splitting rules.
non_obvious_insight: Lawyers treat the house as a property-division problem when it is a loan-portability problem. The low-rate first mortgage is often the most valuable asset in the marriage. Illustratively, keeping $300k at 3% and borrowing $100k at 8.5% blends to about 4.4%, versus about 6.5% on a $400k cash-out refinance, roughly $300 to $400 a month less in payment. Nobody in the divorce process is paid to run that comparison.
first_30_days: Partner with one NMLS-licensed loan officer and two HELOC or second-lien lenders. Publish the calculator and a 'divorce and your mortgage' guide. Offer 5 mediators, divorce attorneys or CDFAs a free house model for their next 10 clients. Process 5 live cases and build servicer-by-servicer playbooks on assumption timelines and release requirements. Then sell the flat-fee plan to DIY-divorce customers.

title: Vacant Inherited-Home Insurance and Caretaking
one_liner: A bundled insurance-plus-sensors-plus-caretaker program for the house that sits empty during probate.
customer: Executors and heirs of a decedent's home, reached through probate attorneys, funeral homes and hospice social workers. Insurers and MGAs are the capacity partners.
problem: Homeowners policies typically restrict coverage for vandalism, freezing and other perils once a home is vacant 30-60 days, which is exactly when no probate court has appointed anyone. Probate often takes 9-18 months (unverified estimate). A burst pipe or break-in lands on an amateur executor, who may be personally exposed. Property taxes and utilities also keep running.
solution: An MGA-backed 'Estate Home Program' with a vacant-dwelling policy placed with a surplus-lines carrier, water and temperature sensors, weekly visits, lock rekeying and mail handling, utility transfer to the executor, and an optional executor advance for carrying costs repaid at sale. Add clean-out and sale-prep referrals.
why_now: Housing wealth is starting to flow from Boomers. Insurers tightened property underwriting after recent nonrenewal waves, and cheap IoT sensors make monitoring practical.
revenue_model: MGA commission (10-20%), a $150-$300/month program fee, and margin on clean-out and sale-prep referrals.
non_obvious_insight: The house effectively becomes uninsurable at the exact moment the owner dies, and nobody owns that timing gap. Executors find out after the loss.
first_30_days: Find an E&S broker who writes vacant dwellings and design a 'vacant estate' placement. Sign 5 probate attorneys and test with 10 houses. Confirm state vacancy and insurable-interest rules with a licensed agent.

title: Recurring-Route Repricing Desk for Service Owners
one_liner: Read-only connect a lawn, pool, cleaning or pest route to its books, find the customers who are losing money, and hand the owner ready-to-send price-increase letters.
customer: Owners of 2-15 person recurring-service companies (lawn, pool, cleaning, pest, window) on Jobber, Housecall Pro or ServiceM8 plus QuickBooks. They pay a one-time audit fee, then a monthly retainer.
problem: Owners discover their margin problem after the fact. r/sweatystartup: "Profitable jobs on paper keep turning into break-even or worse when I look at the actual numbers after" (82/100). A Jobber Community thread is titled "Anyone else realize they were breaking even or losing money after expenses?", and its owner had a full schedule but jobs barely broke even once true payroll burden (taxes, workers comp), supplies, insurance and transaction fees were counted. Tools do not fix it: Jobber adds job costing only on its $39-199/mo plans, and Joist stops at $8/mo estimates. Fear of losing the client keeps owners from raising prices.
solution: 1) A read-only connection or CSV export of Jobber or Housecall Pro, QuickBooks or Stripe, and payroll. 2) Per-customer true margin, including labor burden, drive time, card fees and callbacks. 3) A ranked list of customers to raise by X%, re-scope or drop. 4) Auto-drafted price-increase notices, phone scripts and rebuttals for the "I'll go elsewhere" reply. 5) A churn tracker that shows what each increase cost or earned. It is sold as a productized service backed by software, not as a dashboard.
why_now: Owners are absorbing cost increases in labor, insurance and materials and cannot afford to keep pricing by feel. LLMs let a two-person team parse messy exports and receipts and allocate costs per customer, which used to take a bookkeeper hours. Incumbent field-service tools keep gating job costing behind upper tiers.
revenue_model: $149 one-time margin audit. $99-199/mo retainer for monthly re-scoring, letters and churn tracking. Optional 10% referral to insurers or payroll partners.
non_obvious_insight: Every field-service tool records revenue. The missing piece is cost allocation and the nerve to raise prices, so the paid deliverable is the letter and the script, not another dashboard. Evidence: r/sweatystartup cluster "Unprofitable Service Jobs" and "How do you price your cleaning jobs? Looking to update my rates" (https://www.ideafast.pro/pains/sweatystartup). The owner-facing forum thread is at https://community.getjobber.com/discussions/finances-forum/anyone-else-realize-they-were-breaking-even-or-losing-money-after-expenses/9694. Job costing is gated to $39-199/mo tiers and estimate tools stop at $8/mo (https://www.microgaps.com/blog/saas-niches-nobody-talking-about-2026). r/smallbusiness shows the fear: "Should I fire a client that's 50% of my revenue?" and "Client sent me a 1-star review because I charged for extra work" (https://www.ideafast.pro/pains/smallbusiness). SaaS is structurally a poor fit for tiny businesses, so a service with custom tooling wins here (https://beekeycheung.substack.com/p/saas-products-leave-small-businesses).
first_30_days: Week 1: post in r/sweatystartup and the Jobber Community offering 10 free margin audits from a CSV export. Weeks 2-3: do them by hand in a spreadsheet and record which customers each owner would raise or drop. Week 4: convert to $149 audits and pre-sell the $99/mo retainer to the first 5. Target 20 paid audits and 5 retainers within the first two months.

title: Fandom Events in Empty Cinema Auditoriums
one_liner: A rights-plus-ticketing agency that fills weekday auditoriums with VTuber concert viewings, esports finals and game-reveal nights, splitting the box office with cinema chains.
customer: Fandom promoters and community organizers, VTuber agencies, esports and game publishers wanting fan events, and regional cinema chains as venue partners. Fans pay $15-30.
problem: Overseas viewers are about 30% of Hololive viewership and roughly 10B yen of revenue, yet have no communal way to attend, while Sphere-scale venues cost hundreds of millions and Live Nation controls arenas. Independent organizers rent bars with poor AV and no rights.
solution: Package a dark room, great sound and a projection booth with the rest of the event: sublicensed rights, a licensed live feed, all-in-price ticketing, cosplay contests and merch tables. Start with regional independent chains and a fixed menu of event formats.
why_now: Hololive concert revenue grew 18.7% and overseas fandom is underserved. The FTC's all-in-pricing rule and the Live Nation verdict make promoters and fans look for alternatives to arena ticketing. Cinemas still need non-Hollywood content for off-peak seats.
revenue_model: 15-25% of ticket revenue plus $2-8k per event for rights and technical fees, with cinemas taking a box-office split and concessions.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce ingredient in experience-economy fandom is not a $2B dome, it's a room with audio and projection, which cinemas already own and leave empty midweek. Everyone is chasing IP-in-space capex while the arbitrage is empty seats.
first_30_days: Pitch 5 independent cinema owners on a revenue split. Sign one rights-cleared event, such as a fighting-game grand finals viewing or a licensed VTuber concert screening. Run three test events by day 45 and measure fill rate and concession spend.
